To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the effect of duration of residence on health is not monotonic, but rather U-shaped, (2) duration of residence is associated with a lower risk of poor health for immigrants who have lived in the US for less than 5 years and for immigrants who have spent at least 20 years in the US, and (3) the effect of the length of residence on immigrant health is not due to differences in the age, gender, and nativity composition of immigrant cohorts.
the negative association between duration and health among immigrants and their children is not robust.

(a) immigrants’ health declines as they become more acculturating and this effect is not due to the length of time immigrants have lived in America; (b) immigrants’ health is not affected by the duration they spent in America, but is affected by their length of time in the United States; (c) immigrants’ health deteriorates as they become more assimilated into American society; and (d) immigrants who assimilate faster have worse health outcomes than those who assimilate more slowly.
In summary, our research is concerned with
re-examining the effect of duration and its relationship to immigrant health.
rethinking the effect of duration of residence on immigrant health.
the effect of duration of residence on the health of immigrants and their children.

the longer immigrants stay in the United States, the worse their health.
immigrants’ health declines as their length of residence in the U.S. increases.
the longer immigrants are exposed to American culture, the worse their health becomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the duration effect is not as strong as we previously thought.

the duration effect is not a simple function of the time that immigrants live in the U.S. but rather a complex function of the time they have been exposed to U.S. society and the extent to which their exposure has changed the nature and intensity of the stress they face.
the effect of duration is not as strong as previously thought.

the effect of duration of U.S. residence on immigrant health is not linear.
duration is not a proxy for the health effects of acculturation.
